newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Violence marks Netanyahu's 100th day in office.
newsitem.headline: Violence marks Netanyahu's 100th day in office.

text.p: Palestinians prepared to mark Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's 100 days in office on Thursday with protests, strikes and funerals for seven Arabs killed in clashes with Israeli troops.

Simmering anger at Netanyahu's delay in extending Palestinian self-rule in the West Bank and Gaza boiled over on Wednesday after his right-wing government's decision to open a tunnel beside Islam's third holiest site in Jerusalem.

Israeli soldiers shot dead seven Palestinians, at least three of them police, in gun battles and clashes with stone-throwers on the edge of the PLO-ruled enclave of Ramallah, north of Jerusalem. Doctors said up to 300 were injured, several critically.
Fierce clashes also erupted in Bethlehem, plunging relations between Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Netanyahu into crisis and unnerving the United States, sponsor of Middle East peacemaking.

Israel's guardian ally Washington mounted a frantic diplomatic effort to defuse the confrontation. Secretary of State Warren Christopher expressed "deep concern" over the clashes and his spokesman urged the sides to avoid raising new issues that could scuttle fragile peace talks.
Rival Palestinian factions issued a joint statement on Wednesday calling for a Palestinian day of mourning and two-hour strikes across the West Bank and Gaza on Thursday.

"(We call on) the Palestinian masses to go out and march in the city centres in all regions. The central march will take place in Ramallah at Manara Square at 10.30 a.m. (0830 GMT) to take part in the funerals of the fighting martyrs who defend Arab Jerusalem," the leaflet said.

The statement, signed by eight Palestinian movements, was the first of its kind since rival factions joined forces in the 1987-1993 intifada or uprising. It called for schools and business to close from 0800 to 1000 GMT.
Wednesday's stone-throwing and tyre-burning brought back memories of that uprising but with one difference -- the presence of 30,000 armed Palestinian police in self-rule areas.
The police came to bolster Arafat and ensure Israeli security after the PLO leader returned to Gaza in July 1994 at the start of a process that Palestinians hoped would lead to an independent state.
But Netanyahu's May election victory thwarted that dream. The Likud leader is offering only functional Palestinian autonomy under overall Israeli control.

Netanyahu, on a European swing, told a rally of French supporters of his right-wing Likud party that Arafat "should calm passions and not inflame them. He should return to the negotiating table and not preach violence."
Senior Israeli defence officials, meeting in emergency session in Netanyahu's absence, ordered the West Bank and Gaza Strip sealed off immediately and "until further notice".
An army spokeswoman said this was done "to allow a calming of passions and to prevent new flareups."
But closures, widely seen as collective punishment, have crippled the Palestinian economy, deepening the plight of Palestinians kept from reaching jobs in Israel.

Frustration on the Palestinian street has been building for months. Netanyahu's "tampering", in Palestinian minds, with the status quo of Moslem holy places in the contested Old City of Jerusalem provided the perfect channel for its expression.
Youths in Ramallah initially cursed Palestinian police for not defending them on Wednesday. But jeers turned to cheers when police and Arafat's Force 17 guards returned fire.
Palestinian sources acknowledged that if the police had stood idly by popular anger would have turned against the Palestinian Authority.

Western officials and left-wing Israelis have long thought that Netanyahu's reluctance to embrace the Oslo peace formula could undermine Arafat, who has brought few tangible benefits to the two million Palestinians of the West Bank and Gaza.
